nameStory: Horsetail Spikerush gets its name from its distinctive jointed stems that look remarkably similar to the segmented stems of horsetail plants (Equisetum). The hollow stems have internal walls called septa that create visible joints, giving the plant a bamboo-like or telescope appearance. This resemblance is so strong that it earned the alternative common name 'jointed spike-rush.'
description: Horsetail Spikerush is a wetland sedge that grows in shallow freshwater areas throughout New England's coastal regions and scattered inland locations. This grass-like plant produces clusters of slender, hollow stems that have a distinctive jointed appearance due to internal cross-walls. The stems are topped with small, brownish flower spikes that give the plant its 'spikerush' name. It's a relatively uncommon plant in New England, making it an exciting find for nature explorers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow, round stems with visible joints created by internal cross-walls (septa) - gently squeeze a stem and you'll feel it's hollow, and look closely to see the segmented appearance like a tiny bamboo

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, brownish spikes at the tips of stems that feel firm and slightly rough to the touch when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps of upright stems emerging from wet soil or shallow water, often growing alongside other wetland sedges and rushes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are reduced to small sheaths at the base of stems - the green stems do most of the photosynthesis work

habitat: Look for Horsetail Spikerush in freshwater marshes, pond edges, and wet meadows, particularly along the coastal plain from Cape Cod south. It prefers areas with standing water or consistently moist, muddy soils. You'll often find it growing with other wetland plants like cattails, other spikerushes, and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: New stems begin emerging from the muddy substrate, initially soft and bright green. The jointed structure becomes more apparent as stems lengthen.
seasonality.summer: Flowering spikes develop at stem tips, and the distinctive hollow, jointed stems are at their most visible and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn brown and release seeds, while stems begin to yellow and become more brittle to the touch.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist above ground, still showing the characteristic jointed pattern, though they'll be brown and fragile.

funFact: This plant is like nature's drinking straw - the hollow stems with internal walls work as a snorkel system, allowing air to travel down to the roots even when they're completely underwater, which is essential for survival in oxygen-poor wetland mud.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with true horsetails (Equisetum species), which have similar jointed stems but feel rough and gritty due to silica deposits - horsetails will make a scratching sound when rubbed together, while Horsetail Spikerush stems are smooth. Remember: if it's gritty, it's a horsetail; if it's smooth and topped with a brown spike, it's a spikerush.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Horsetail Spikerush is not related to true horsetails at all - it's a sedge in the same family as cotton grass and bulrushes, while horsetails are ancient fern relatives. This is a classic example of convergent evolution, where unrelated plants develop similar features to solve the same environmental challenges.
compareHints: Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments. The related species that shares this jointed feature (E. interstincta) doesn't occur in New England, making the jointed stems a reliable identification feature in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
